presenceLabel: Fort Ancient area (archaeological culture, not a tribe)
presenceNote: An archaeological culture, not a tribe: farming villages in the middle Ohio Valley that archaeologists group as Fort Ancient, about AD 1000–1750. Drawn: ten whole Kentucky counties with documented villages. A general area, not a boundary; the Ohio, Indiana and West Virginia parts are not drawn and no village locations are shown. Medium confidence (years high, area medium).
overlapNote: Fort Ancient villages lie in the same Kentucky counties as Adena and the Shawnee area, but in different centuries for Adena; some late Fort Ancient years overlap the 1700s Shawnee, Mosopelea, Miami and Mingo areas, and the year slider keeps them apart. No descent from or link to any later people is claimed.
basis: Kentucky Archaeological Survey Fort Ancient booklet, the Kentucky Heritage Council Mississippi-period chapter (for the boundary with Mississippian western Kentucky), and Wikipedia (Fort Ancient). Public agency sources.

eras.label: 1000–1199 CE · Early Fort Ancient
eras.text: Fort Ancient is an archaeological culture, a group of sites that archaeologists define from the pottery, village layouts and dates they share; it is not a tribe, and no descent from or link to any later people is claimed. The Kentucky Archaeological Survey places the Fort Ancient tradition (about AD 1000–1750) in central, northern and eastern Kentucky, with parts of southeastern Indiana, southwestern Ohio and western West Virginia. The tint is ten whole Kentucky counties with documented Fort Ancient villages (Boone, Bracken, Mason, Harrison, Bourbon, Scott, Jessamine, Madison, Estill, Greenup). The sources do not list the full set of Fort Ancient counties, so this is a general area, not a boundary; the Ohio, Indiana and West Virginia parts are not drawn, and village locations are not shown. This is the early period, from about AD 1000 to 1200.
